cues.text:
You are in the decision meeting. Before
opening the scorecard,

read the rules the team approved at
kickoff.

Expand when the benefit and guardrails
are met. Adjust when a specific issue
can be addressed in a bounded follow-up.

Pause for a serious data or access
incident,

or when the quality risk needs
investigation before continuing.

This sequence matters because a strong
speed result is easy to focus on.

Put all three decisions on the table.
Ask a teammate which evidence would make

them choose each one before showing the
pilot numbers.

Walk down the scorecard. Wait is
thirteen business hours against
fourteen.

Active review is twenty-six minutes
against twenty-seven.

Spending is two hundred and forty
dollars against three hundred.

Each clears its threshold. Seven of
forty requests needed rework,

so that row lands at seventeen and a
half percent.

The ceiling was fifteen. The defect
count is one in each group,

and there were zero serious data or
access incidents.

The rework row rules out expansion under
the team's agreement.

Now check whether it gives you a clear
change to try.

Pull up the review notes. Four of the
seven rework cases included files
outside the intended change.

In one of those cases the reviewer asked
to drop unrelated formatting.

Turn that observation into two concrete
steps.

The author lists the expected files in
Copilot Plan and checks every actual

changed path before publishing the
branch.

If a third file appears, the author asks
what it contributes to the stated
acceptance criteria.

The independent reviewer still checks
the final pull request.

This is an adjustment the team can
observe in the follow-up.

The engineering lead owns the next four
weeks.

Keep the service, eligibility, and
metric definitions in place so the next
readout can be compared with the pilot.

At forty requests, six rework cases
would meet fifteen percent.

If only thirty requests qualify, four
cases equal about thirteen point three

percent and five equal about sixteen
point seven.

Use the actual denominator. Check the
reason each time work comes back.

You need evidence that the extra-file
pattern improved,

together with the time and spending
measures that supported the original
pilot.

Try three short scenarios. First, the
follow-up meets the wait, effort,
rework, and budget thresholds.

Propose expansion to one comparable team
and name its onboarding owner.

Second, one routine guardrail misses by
a little and review evidence points to a
fixable cause.

Consider another bounded adjustment.
Third, someone sends restricted data to
an unapproved model endpoint.

Pause the affected workflow and use the
existing incident process.

Practice saying each decision with the
evidence that triggered it.

The person who owns the next action
should hear exactly what to do.

Open a decision record and fill in a
date, an owner, the decision,
and the next review.

For this case we choose adjust. Median
wait met the target, rework did not,

and the extra-file pattern gives us a
focused intervention.

Name the engineering lead, attach the
scorecard and the review evidence,

and put a follow-up on the calendar four
weeks from the relaunch.
Then hand the note to a teammate.

If they can tell which workflow to
change and what evidence will determine
the next decision, the record is ready.
